questions: With the 0.10 m track and 0.6 kg mass, does the robot still leave the line early, and at what progress and curvature?
Does steering oscillation increase on the slalom compared with the 0.12 m / 0.8 kg baseline?
Is the 5-sensor row (15 mm spacing) still giving a clean, monotonic signal, or do the readings saturate at high lateral error?
Is the 50 mm forward lead enough on the s-bend, or does the signal arrive too late for the correction to work?
feedback_request.requested_changes_if_any: If the robot is still off track early with lower yaw inertia, state whether the limiting factor is the sensor lead or the base_speed/turn gain combination, so I can change the next geometry parameter.

intent: Test whether a faster-responding body (narrower wheel track 0.10 m, lighter 0.6 kg) reduces off-track departures seen in iteration 0. Sensor row, lead and body are unchanged so the drivetrain effect is isolated. Expected result: max_error below 0.06 m and more progress on the oval and s-bend. If the slalom oscillates more, the next step is to restore some mass or track width rather than change the sensors.
learning: Iteration 0 showed all runs ending off track at about 11-16% progress. Body width cannot raise the 0.06 m off-track limit, so the next change targets drivetrain responsiveness. The result will show whether yaw response or sensor lead is the binding constraint.
rationale: The development race for iteration 0 has no completions. All 60 trials ended off track after about 11-16% progress, with max_error near 0.06-0.07 m. With body_width 0.12 the off-track limit is max(0.06, 0.0125 + 0.03) = 0.06 m. Widening the body cannot raise that limit above 0.06 m (a 0.18 m body still gives 0.0575 m), so the limit is fixed and the robot must keep its error smaller. The early failures point to a slow corrective response rather than to the sensor row losing the line: the line loss count is 1 per run, and the failure happens well before the course ends. The yaw response is set by wheel_track and mass. Yaw inertia is mass*(L^2+W^2)/12, and turn rate is the wheel speed difference divided by wheel_track. A narrower track gives more yaw per PWM difference, and a lighter robot has less inertia to resist it. I therefore change only the drivetrain response this iteration: wheel_track from 0.12 to 0.10 m and mass from 0.8 to 0.6 kg. The sensor row, its 50 mm lead and body are kept fixed so the effect can be read cleanly. I expect max_error to fall below 0.06 m on the oval and s-bend, which would let runs go further, with a risk of more steering oscillation on the slalom. This is an isolated test, not a final design.
